One commenter said everyone who avoided React did so because of the license, so they should be happy now that the BSD+Patents license is being replaced.

A skeptic said the relicensing doesn't solve anything: BSD was swapped for MIT, which are basically the same, and the explicit patent grant was removed, so users are 'actually granted less rights than before.'
Several users asked why Facebook chose MIT instead of Apache 2.0. They noted the new license has no explicit patent grant, and whether MIT implies one is not legally settled.
A user credited WordPress's public stance against React's license for prompting the change. Others noted some big players had already abandoned React for Vue or other frameworks over the license.
A developer who wrote a React-like TUI library for Clojure said reading the React source to understand how React works is very challenging.

One commenter called concurrent mode and fibers 'kludgy hacks' that stem from only the main thread having DOM access. They said few other frameworks schedule DOM updates as aggressively as React, and those frameworks are simpler to understand as a result.

A user praised the React team's own DOM manipulation abstraction, with efficient change management and no interruption of the main JS thread. They said it could be a general-purpose approach that might eventually replace how the DOM works.
A commenter praised Sophie Alpert's talk on building custom renderers through React's exposed interfaces. They said it shows React can serve as a declarative API for pretty much any platform.
